stories.headline: Update: Tropical Storm Arthur Brings Life-Threatening Flash Flooding to Gulf Coast and Southeast
stories.summary:
Tropical Storm Arthur, the first named storm of the 2026 Atlantic hurricane season, formed off the Texas coast Wednesday and has since weakened to a low-pressure system, but continues to pose a serious flooding threat across the Gulf Coast and southeastern United States. Forecasters warned of life-threatening flash flooding, with rainfall totals of five to ten inches expected across parts of Texas, Mississippi, and Louisiana, and isolated totals of up to twenty inches in some areas.

The National Hurricane Center said the highest flash flood potential over the coming days stretches from Lake Charles, Louisiana, to Montgomery, Alabama, with Mobile, Alabama, expected to see the heaviest rainfall. Brazoria County on the Texas Gulf Coast recorded winds of 55 mph Wednesday morning as the storm moved through.

Texas Governor Greg Abbott had already issued a disaster declaration for 101 counties earlier this month due to severe storms. Atmospheric scientists noted that parts of the Southeast had endured prolonged drought conditions this spring, leaving soils now saturated and particularly vulnerable to rapid runoff and localized flooding.

The storm is also affecting the FIFA World Cup, which is hosting matches in Houston and Atlanta. Houston canceled its FIFA Fan Festival on Monday due to rain, though officials said the matches themselves were not expected to be significantly disrupted.

stories.headline: U.S. Military Strike on Alleged Drug Boat Kills Three in Eastern Pacific, Bringing Total Deaths to at Least 211
stories.summary:
The U.S. military struck a boat in the eastern Pacific Ocean on Thursday that it described as operating along known narco-trafficking routes, killing three people. The strike is the latest in a campaign the Trump administration launched in early September, during which at least 211 people have been killed in military attacks on boats the Pentagon has labeled as belonging to designated terrorist organizations.

U.S. Southern Command announced the strike via social media but did not provide evidence the vessel was carrying drugs, nor did it identify which specific cartel or organization was alleged to be operating it. Video posted publicly showed the vessel being struck and bursting into flames.

President Trump has described the U.S. as being in "armed conflict" with cartels and justified the strikes as essential to stopping the flow of drugs and fatal overdoses into the United States. Critics, including Colombian President Gustavo Petro, have questioned both the legality and effectiveness of the strategy, noting that fentanyl — responsible for the majority of overdose deaths — is primarily trafficked over land from Mexico rather than by sea.

Senators on Thursday formally demanded that the Pentagon release unedited video of the strikes. The Pentagon's inspector general announced in May it was reviewing whether the military followed proper targeting frameworks, with particular scrutiny on an early strike in which survivors clinging to wreckage were killed in a follow-up attack the White House described as self-defense.

stories.headline: New York Knicks Celebrated With Canyon of Heroes Parade, First Championship in 53 Years
stories.summary:
Hundreds of thousands of fans flooded lower Manhattan on Thursday for a ticker-tape parade celebrating the New York Knicks' first NBA championship in 53 years. Finals MVP Jalen Brunson held the golden trophy aloft along the Canyon of Heroes as blue and orange confetti filled the air and crowds chanted "Let's go, Knicks!"

At a City Hall ceremony following the parade, New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani presented keys to the city to players, coaches, owners, and staff. Mamdani, who wore a team jersey under his suit, said fans had "waited because we knew deep down in our sick, suffering hearts" the Knicks would eventually win.

Filmmaker Spike Lee, among the team's most iconic fans, rode a float with Brunson and said it was his first championship parade. Forward OG Anunoby, who scored the decisive basket in Game 4 with 1.2 seconds remaining, left his float to interact directly with fans on the parade route.

The title ends a drought that stretches back to the Knicks' 1973 championship. Owner James Dolan thanked fans for their patience, while coach Mike Brown urged the crowd to sustain its energy for future seasons.

stories.headline: FDA Panel Unanimously Backs First mRNA Flu Vaccine for Older Americans
stories.summary:
A Food and Drug Administration advisory committee voted unanimously Thursday that Moderna's mRNA-based influenza vaccine, dubbed mFlusiva, shows benefits that outweigh its risks for Americans aged 50 and older. The panel's endorsement moves the shot — the first flu vaccine made with the mRNA technology that underpinned COVID-19 vaccines — a step closer to U.S. market approval ahead of the winter flu season. The FDA will consider the recommendation in making a final decision by early August.

Moderna is seeking full approval for use in people ages 50 to 64 and emergency authorization for those 65 and older while additional testing continues. In a study of 40,000 people, the mRNA vaccine reduced flu cases by roughly 27 percent compared with another routinely used vaccine. A separate study in those 65 and older showed a strong protective immune response relative to a high-dose flu vaccine already recommended for that group.

Experts cited the technology's key advantage: mRNA vaccines can be manufactured far more quickly than conventional flu shots, a critical capability if a new flu strain emerges that requires an updated formulation on short notice. Tens of thousands of Americans die from influenza each year, with older adults among the most vulnerable. FDA advisers called the immune response data "very compelling" and said the vaccine "looks very promising."

The approval process comes as the mRNA platform, already normalized through COVID-19, faces renewed scrutiny from vaccine-skeptical voices in the current political environment. Supporters argue the technology represents a generational leap in pandemic preparedness; critics have raised concerns about long-term data on mRNA products. The FDA's final ruling is expected before the start of the fall flu season.

stories.headline: Obama Presidential Center Subcontractors Claim Millions in Unpaid Bills Ahead of Grand Opening
stories.summary:
Multiple construction firms that helped build the Obama Presidential Center in Chicago say they are facing financial ruin after being left with millions of dollars in unpaid bills, according to a Fox News Digital investigation published Thursday. The allegations surface days before the center's scheduled grand opening Friday, and directly undercut one of the project's central promises: to uplift minority-owned and local businesses through one of Chicago's most high-profile construction projects.

Among those cited is Adamson Plumbing, whose owner Mike Owen says his firm is owed nearly $4 million. Several other firms described a chaotic work environment marked by repeated design changes, scheduling disruptions, and prolonged compensation disputes. Some declined to speak on the record, citing confidentiality agreements or fear of professional retaliation. Overall construction costs, reported at $830 million in 2021, are believed to have surpassed $1 billion.

The report follows a separate Fox News Digital investigation revealing that the Obama Foundation's reserve fund — promoted as a $470 million financial safeguard for taxpayers — remains funded at roughly $1 million. Critics argue the gap between the project's stated mission of economic empowerment and the reported nonpayment of minority-owned firms represents a significant credibility problem for the foundation.

The Obama Foundation has not issued a detailed public response to the payment claims. Supporters of the project note that large construction undertakings routinely involve disputes between general contractors and subcontractors, and that the center's opening represents a historic milestone for Chicago's South Side community. Legal and financial proceedings related to the payment claims are ongoing.

stories.headline: Suspected Gang Leader Shot Dead in Flower Bouquet Ambush at Ecuador Airport
stories.summary:
A man identified by Ecuadorean police as the leader of the Los Águilas gang was shot and killed Wednesday at the arrivals terminal of Guayaquil's airport, the country's largest city, in a brazen daylight ambush. Security footage shows two young men posing as greeters — holding stuffed animals and flowers — before one pulled a firearm from behind a teddy bear and shot the victim at point-blank range. Police have detained two teenagers in connection with the killing.

The victim, identified as 39-year-old Carlos Alberto Suástegui Villanueva, was described by Ecuador's interior minister as the regional leader of Los Águilas, a gang designated a terrorist organization by President Daniel Noboa in 2024. The group is accused of involvement in drug trafficking and extortion across central Ecuador. The arrivals hall was closed for more than two hours as forensic teams processed the scene; one bystander was wounded.

The attack came just one day after Noboa declared a fresh state of emergency in 10 provinces, including Guayas, where the shooting occurred. Despite repeated emergency declarations granting security forces expanded search powers, Ecuador's murder rate reached a record high in 2025. The country has transformed over recent years from a relatively stable nation into one of the Western Hemisphere's most violent, driven by its position as a key cocaine transit corridor between Colombia, Peru, and global markets.

The public nature of the assault — carried out in front of arriving passengers who fled in panic — underscored the degree to which criminal organizations are willing to operate openly even as the government escalates its security response. Analysts warn that targeted killings of gang leaders often trigger internal succession violence rather than reducing overall criminal activity.

stories.headline: Tourist, 18, Dies After Runaway Horse-Drawn Carriage Overturns in Central Park
stories.summary:
An 18-year-old tourist from India, Romanch Mahajan, died Wednesday after a horse-drawn carriage carrying passengers broke free and bolted through New York City's Central Park, striking another carriage and overturning near Tavern on the Green at West 72nd Street. Mahajan was transported to a hospital in critical condition and later pronounced dead. The NYPD said the investigation remains ongoing and officials have not determined what caused the horse to become spooked.

Preliminary information from the union representing carriage drivers, TWU Local 100, suggests the driver may have stepped away from the horse to photograph passengers before the animal took off. Union representative Alexander Kemp called the alleged behavior "unacceptable," stating drivers are never supposed to leave the carriage. The union said it supports a full investigation and is calling for enhanced driver training and stricter rules governing new horses entering the business.

The fatal incident immediately reignited a long-running debate over the future of New York City's horse-drawn carriage industry. The Central Park Conservancy, which has previously opposed the practice, called for changes in the wake of the death. Animal welfare advocates have sought to ban the carriages for years, arguing the urban environment poses inherent dangers to horses and passengers alike; the industry and its labor representatives have countered that the trade is a historic part of New York's culture and supports working-class jobs.

The incident drew coverage from more than 20 national and international outlets, reflecting both its human tragedy and its resonance as a recurring policy dispute in one of the world's most-visited cities. No charges have been announced.

stories.headline: 35 Killed as Gunmen Storm Niger's Largest Airport in Second Attack in Five Months
stories.summary:
Gunmen attacked Diori Hamani International Airport in Niamey, Niger's capital, early Thursday morning, killing 35 people, including 22 assailants, 11 soldiers, and two civilians, according to the country's defense ministry. The assault began shortly after morning prayers, with residents describing the sounds of explosions and gunfire before dawn. Security forces repelled the attack and launched a subsequent manhunt for surviving attackers, some of whom reportedly blended into the surrounding civilian population.

The airport serves as both a civilian aviation hub and a military base, and also hosts facilities linked to the Alliance of Sahel States, the bloc comprising Niger, Mali, and Burkina Faso — all three governed by military juntas. This is the second attack on the same airport in less than five months; in January, an assault claimed by an Islamic State-linked organization wounded four military personnel and killed 20 attackers.

Niger has battled an Islamist insurgency for a decade, and authorities had recently taken steps to harden the airport's security, including extending its perimeter fence and installing more than 350 surveillance cameras. No group has yet claimed responsibility for Thursday's attack. Armed local residents joined the manhunt despite efforts by security personnel to keep civilians from engaging.

The assault is the latest sign that the Sahel's military-led governments, which came to power in part by promising to better address jihadist violence, continue to face severe security challenges. Niger's junta leader previously thanked Russia for its assistance in foiling the January attack.

stories.headline: National Gas Average Drops Below $4 a Gallon for First Time Since March
stories.summary:
The U.S. national average price for a gallon of regular gasoline fell to $3.99 on Thursday, the lowest level since March 30, according to AAA data. The drop follows months of elevated pump prices driven by Iran's disruption of oil traffic through the Strait of Hormuz, which had rattled global energy markets. Crude oil prices in June fell to their lowest point in more than three months following news of an extended ceasefire agreement between the U.S. and Iran.

President Trump signed an agreement with Iran requiring Tehran to dilute its stockpile of highly enriched uranium in exchange for the waiving of certain U.S.-backed sanctions. The deal is designed to restore normal shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, a critical chokepoint for global oil supply, though analysts caution that full price relief will take additional time as tanker traffic normalizes.

The decline offers tangible economic relief to American consumers who have faced sustained pain at the pump throughout the spring. Analysts expect prices to continue declining through the summer if the ceasefire holds and shipping lanes fully reopen, though the situation remains fragile given the renewed Iran-Israel military exchange reported Thursday.

The gas price drop represents one of the first direct consumer benefits of the U.S.-Iran diplomatic effort, and is likely to factor into public assessments of the administration's economic performance at a time when polls show Trump's economic approval ratings under pressure.

stories.headline: Hegseth Announces Six-Month Review of U.S. Forces in Europe, Calls for 'NATO 3.0'
stories.summary:
U.S. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth traveled to Brussels on Thursday and announced a sweeping six-month review of American troop deployments across Europe, pressing NATO allies to assume primary responsibility for their own defense. Hegseth called for a fundamental restructuring of the alliance, branding his vision 'NATO 3.0' and signaling that Washington intends to substantially reduce its security commitments to the continent.

The announcement follows a recent U.S. decision to scale back its commitments to a NATO high-readiness force, and comes as the alliance is already under strain from the ongoing war in Ukraine and questions about long-term American engagement in European security. Hegseth said the review would include consultations with Congress, suggesting potential legislative dimensions to any changes in force posture.

The move represents one of the most direct challenges to the post-World War II U.S.-European security architecture in decades. European allies have been pressing member states to dramatically increase defense spending, with the war in Ukraine having already accelerated rearmament plans across the continent. Critics warn that signaling a potential drawdown of U.S. forces could embolden Russia at a moment of active conflict; supporters argue European nations must bear a greater share of their own defense burden.

The announcement carries major geopolitical implications for tens of millions of people across NATO member states and arrives at a moment when the U.S.-Iran deal is simultaneously reshaping Middle East security commitments, raising broader questions about the direction of American foreign and defense policy.

stories.headline: Student Loan Defaults Surge to 9.2 Million as Federal Collections Resume
stories.summary:
The number of student loan borrowers in default has soared to approximately 9.2 million people, according to the latest data from the U.S. Department of Education, as the federal government ended a four-year pandemic-era pause on collections that had shielded borrowers since the onset of COVID-19. The sharp rise represents one of the largest surges in student loan default figures in the program's history.

The Trump administration's resumption of collections has been a central policy reversal from the Biden-era approach, which had repeatedly extended relief for borrowers and pursued broad debt cancellation programs that were partially blocked by courts. Supporters of resumed collections argue the pause was a costly and legally questionable extension of emergency authority that unfairly burdened taxpayers; critics contend that restarting collections before adequate income-driven repayment infrastructure was in place has pushed millions of vulnerable borrowers into default with severe credit and financial consequences.

Borrowers in default face consequences including wage garnishment, seizure of tax refunds, and damage to credit scores that can affect housing and employment. Advocacy groups have warned that the spike disproportionately affects lower-income borrowers and those who attended for-profit institutions. The administration has maintained that borrowers have had ample time and access to repayment options.

The 9.2 million figure covers defaults recorded through April and is expected to rise further as collections infrastructure ramps up. The data adds concrete scale to what has been a politically contentious debate over student debt policy, with direct financial consequences for millions of American households.

stories.headline: Ukraine Launches Largest Drone Attack on Moscow Since Start of Full-Scale War
stories.summary:
Ukraine struck Moscow with close to 200 drones on Thursday in the largest attack on the Russian capital since Russia's full-scale invasion began in February 2022. The assault wounded 17 people in the Moscow region, set the Kapotnya oil refinery ablaze for the third time in a month, and forced the temporary closure of all four Moscow airports with more than 500 flights cancelled or delayed. Russia's defense ministry said nearly 1,000 drones and four cruise missiles were intercepted across the country in 24 hours.

President Volodymyr Zelensky framed the strike as direct retaliation for a Russian attack on Kyiv last week that set a major religious landmark on fire. "If Ukraine burns, your Moscow will burn too," he said, while calling on Russia to take steps toward diplomacy to end the war. An oil depot in the southern Rostov region was also struck, killing one person.

The attack marks a significant escalation in Ukraine's campaign to bring the war to Russian civilians and infrastructure hundreds of kilometers from the front lines. Ukraine has steadily expanded its long-range drone capabilities since its first strikes reached Moscow in spring 2023, and analysts note that the sheer volume of drones now deployed is increasingly overwhelming Russian air defenses despite extensive systems around the capital.

The strike comes as global attention is focused on the newly signed U.S.-Iran memorandum of understanding, which has raised questions about the broader trajectory of major conflicts. Russia's military separately reported that Ukraine fired hundreds of additional drones across the country overnight, underscoring the intensity of Kyiv's long-range offensive strategy.

stories.headline: Update: Federal Reserve Holds Rates Steady in Warsh's First Meeting; Officials Signal Possible Hike Later This Year
stories.summary:
The Federal Reserve held its benchmark interest rate unchanged at 3.5 to 3.75 percent at its June meeting, the fourth consecutive hold, marking new Chairman Kevin Warsh's first rate decision since taking over the central bank three weeks ago. All 12 members of the Federal Open Market Committee voted to maintain rates, but new quarterly projections showed that nearly half of policymakers now anticipate a rate hike before year's end — a hawkish signal reflecting persistent inflation concerns.

Warsh signaled that significant structural changes to how the Fed communicates and conducts policy are underway. Notably, he appeared not to have submitted his own interest-rate-path projection in the quarterly forecasts, a break from past practice that analysts said could foreshadow the "regime change" he has promised. The Fed's policy statement was also notably shorter and simpler than past versions. "You might have already noticed something, a difference in today's policy statement," Warsh said at his post-meeting press conference.

The decision comes against a backdrop of renewed inflation fueled in part by the Iran war's disruption of global energy and shipping markets. Warsh, a Trump appointee, takes the helm at a moment when the Fed faces pressure from both rising prices and a slowing economy, and when the Supreme Court has a pending case on the president's ability to remove Fed board members.

Markets reacted to Warsh's refusal to provide explicit forward guidance by pricing in a higher probability of rate increases. Economists say the shift in tone from the previous Fed leadership — which had leaned toward eventual cuts — represents a meaningful departure, though Warsh's ultimate policy path remains uncertain given the rapidly changing economic environment tied to the Iran deal's implementation.

stories.headline: Apple Warns of Unavoidable Price Increases as AI Boom Drives Memory Chip Costs to Record Highs
stories.summary:
Apple CEO Tim Cook told the Wall Street Journal on Thursday that price increases on Apple products are "unavoidable" as surging memory chip costs have made the current situation "unsustainable." Cook cited a dramatic supply-demand imbalance — with RAM prices more than doubling since October 2025 — driven by surging artificial intelligence demand and supply chain disruptions tied to the Iran war's impact on helium, a key semiconductor manufacturing input. He did not specify which products would be affected or when increases would take effect, leaving open the question of whether the iPhone 18, expected in September, will carry higher price tags.

The global smartphone market is already feeling the pressure: the average selling price of smartphones worldwide is expected to rise roughly 20 percent in 2026 to an all-time high, according to research firm Omdia. Apple's new phones could cost up to $150 more than the iPhone 17 lineup, the firm projects, as Apple upgrades hardware specifications to support new AI features. Most major smartphone brands have already raised prices, cut specifications, or pulled back on promotions.

Separately, President Trump announced on Thursday that Apple had agreed to partner with Intel to manufacture chips domestically, writing on Truth Social: "I decided to help Intel because we need to design and build our Chips right here in America." Intel shares surged more than 10 percent on the news. Apple and Intel did not immediately respond to requests for comment. The U.S. government holds a 10 percent stake in Intel following an August 2025 announcement by the Trump administration.

The disclosures signal a broader reckoning across the consumer electronics industry as AI infrastructure investment reshapes semiconductor supply chains and costs flow through to end consumers. Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company, which produces Apple's most advanced chips, separately told the BBC this month it would not rule out its own price increases as inflation pressures mount.

stories.headline: FBI Arrests Five Men Who Allegedly Plotted Drone and Sniper Attack on White House UFC Event
stories.summary:
The FBI has arrested five men across four states on charges of conspiracy to commit murder after uncovering an alleged plot to attack last Sunday's UFC Freedom 250 event on the White House South Lawn using explosive-laden drones and a sniper team. Federal prosecutors allege the group planned to deploy drones to strike nearby buildings and cause panic, funneling the crowd of an estimated 4,300 attendees toward waiting snipers in a "second wave" assault intended to storm the White House gate. Court filings identify alleged targets including President Trump, Vice President Vance, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and Elon Musk, though not all were present at the event.

The five suspects — Tycen C. Proper, 19, of Ohio; Bryan Omar Roa, 24, and Michael Alan Thomas, 32, of California; Daniel K. Eskridge, 32, of Missouri; and Abraham Hermosillo Alvarez, 31, of Nebraska — are each charged with conspiracy to commit murder. The plot was discovered after Proper's mother called local authorities on June 10, alarmed by her son's large firearms purchases and online communications with a group she believed was made up of former military members. During an FBI interview the following day, Proper admitted to the planning and said the group had formed in March through a TikTok group called "Vanguard of the Old Republic."

Prosecutors allege the group expressed "ultra-religious and anti-government sentiments" and sought to "jumpstart" a revolution by killing wealthy people and politicians. Court documents say members specifically discussed grievances over government corruption, the handling of the Epstein files and data center water usage. FBI Director Kash Patel said the "planned attacks were stopped cold" in a social media post announcing the multi-state operation. It remains unclear whether the group is affiliated with any larger established organization.

The alleged plot represents one of the most serious domestic terrorism threats to materialize against a sitting president in recent memory and has intensified scrutiny of radicalization pathways on social media platforms. Alvarez is named in charging documents as the primary organizer. The Justice Department has not publicly characterized the ideological orientation of the group beyond the court filings' descriptions of their stated grievances.

stories.headline: Update: Trump Says U.S.-Iran Deal to Be Signed 'Shortly' as Strait of Hormuz Tensions Persist
stories.summary:
President Trump announced at a news conference in Evian-les-Bains, France, that a deal with Iran would be signed "shortly" — potentially as soon as Thursday. The agreement, described by Vice President Vance as "about a page and a half" and "very general," contains 14 points including an end to fighting, a commitment that Iran will never acquire a nuclear weapon, and a $300 billion redevelopment package for Iran. Both sides agreed to hold further talks on a final agreement within 60 days; the fate of Iran's nuclear program remains to be negotiated in those subsequent talks.

The announcement comes as Iran seized two cargo ships in the Strait of Hormuz, a move that followed Trump's declaration of a U.S. blockade of the waterway. Iranian negotiators have said Tehran "will decide the right of passage" through the strait, and the waterway remains largely closed as ships wait in the Gulf. Energy markets have experienced sharp swings since the U.S. and Israel attacked Iran on February 28.

Trump also said Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu needed "to be more responsible with respect to Lebanon," a signal of U.S.-Israeli friction. Many Lebanese remain skeptical that the broader agreement will end fighting between Israel and Hezbollah. An earlier Israeli strike on Beirut had threatened to derail the deal before it reached its current stage.

For Iranians, the central question is whether the deal will reduce prices and the fear of renewed war rather than who claimed victory. Hard-liners in Tehran have pushed back against the agreement, and the Iranian government faces the challenge of selling its terms to a divided domestic audience. The conflict has already raised global energy costs, with gas prices in the U.S. running roughly 79 cents higher per gallon than a year ago.

stories.headline: Trump's Economic Approval Rating Falls to Record Low in New Poll
stories.summary:
A new PBS NewsHour/NPR/Marist poll finds that only 33 percent of Americans approve of President Trump's handling of the economy, the lowest figure recorded since Marist began asking the question in 2019. Sixty percent of Americans overall disapprove. The result is also lower than the lowest economic approval rating recorded for former President Biden during his term.

The slide is being driven in part by persistent pain at the gas pump and rising food costs. Gas prices remain about 79 cents per gallon higher than a year ago, and 78 percent of Americans said gas prices have affected their household budgets. Notably, 54 percent of white voters without a college degree — a group Trump won decisively in 2024 — now disapprove of his economic handling.

Trump's supporters, however, largely remain with him: 77 percent of those who voted for him in 2024 still approve of his economic stewardship. Analysts note that some supporters who blamed high prices on Biden may now attribute them to corporate price gouging rather than to Trump's policies, partially cushioning his numbers within his base.

Trump's economic credibility was a central pillar of his 2024 campaign. The erosion of that advantage — particularly among working-class voters — marks a significant shift heading toward the 2026 midterms. Gas prices have dropped about 50 cents per gallon from their recent peak, but analysts say many consumers have not yet registered that relief.

stories.headline: Trump Poised to Roll Out New Tariffs as Treasury Refunds Nearly $22 Billion in Unlawful Duties
stories.summary:
The U.S. Treasury disbursed nearly $22 billion in reimbursements to importers in May alone for tariffs courts have ruled were unlawfully collected, meaning tariff revenue is currently flowing out of government coffers faster than it is coming in. The administration is simultaneously preparing to introduce a new round of tariffs, according to Bloomberg, raising questions about the coherence of trade policy at a moment of acute economic sensitivity.

Critics argue the original tariff structure was an "inexplicable mix" that failed to achieve the stated goal of leveraging reciprocal market openings from trading partners. Supporters of the approach have argued that strategic tariffs can paradoxically expand economic freedom by forcing negotiations, though that outcome has not materialized in practice according to analysts cited in the reporting.

The developments add complexity to Trump's economic standing. His administration has repeatedly pointed to tariffs as a tool for rebuilding American manufacturing and extracting concessions from rivals, but the combination of court-ordered refunds and new levies signals ongoing legal and political turbulence around the policy. U.S. trading partners are closely watching what new tariff actions take shape.

The tariff situation intersects with the broader inflation picture that is already weighing on Trump's approval ratings. Higher import costs have contributed to elevated prices for consumer goods, and any fresh round of tariffs could add further upward pressure at a politically difficult moment for the administration.

stories.headline: Gunfire and Explosions Reported at Airport in Niger's Capital Niamey
stories.summary:
Residents of Niamey told the BBC that gunfire and explosions erupted early Thursday morning at the entrance of Diori Hamani International Airport in Niger's capital, with the exchange lasting approximately two hours beginning around 6 a.m. local time. Niger's army is reported to have repelled the attack and is now hunting fleeing assailants who allegedly abandoned their weapons at the scene. Authorities had not officially commented as of initial reports.

The attack follows a near-identical assault on the same airport in January, which an affiliate of the Islamic State claimed responsibility for. In that incident, four military personnel were injured and 20 attackers were killed. Niger's military government, in power for three years, thanked Russia for assistance in foiling the January attack and accused leaders of France, Benin, and Ivory Coast of backing the assailants — accusations for which no evidence was provided.

Niger has been battling a jihadist insurgency for a decade and, alongside neighbors Burkina Faso and Mali, is governed by a military junta that came to power partly on the failure of civilian governments to contain the violence. In recent weeks, Niamey authorities demolished neighborhoods near the airport citing terrorist risks and expanded the perimeter fence and surveillance infrastructure around the facility.

The recurrence of attacks on the same strategic site underscores the fragility of security in the Sahel region and the limits of both military governance and Russian security assistance in containing Islamist militancy across West Africa.
